title: Biomolecules
tagline: Carbohydrates from glucose to starch, amino acids and protein structure, vitamins and their deficiency diseases, and the DNA-RNA difference.

overview.intro: Biomolecules are the organic compounds that make up living organisms and carry out their chemistry: carbohydrates for energy and structure, proteins for catalysis and structure, nucleic acids for the storage and transmission of genetic information, and vitamins and hormones for regulation. The unit approaches them as organic chemistry rather than as biology, so the questions are about functional groups, linkages and the reactions that reveal structure. Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes and ketones, classified as monosaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides, and as reducing or non-reducing according to whether a free anomeric centre is available. The structure of glucose is established from a series of reactions, each of which answers one structural question: heating with hydriodic acid gives n-hexane and proves a straight six-carbon chain, bromine water oxidation proves the aldehyde group, acetic anhydride proves five hydroxyl groups, nitric acid oxidation proves the arrangement of the ends, and phenylhydrazine gives an osazone. Proteins are polymers of alpha-amino acids joined by peptide bonds, and their structure is described at four levels, with denaturation as the loss of the higher levels without breaking the peptide bonds. Vitamins are classified as fat-soluble or water-soluble, each with a characteristic deficiency disease, and nucleic acids are polymers of nucleotides whose bases pair specifically in the DNA double helix.

learningOutcomes: Define carbohydrates and classify them as monosaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides, and as aldoses and ketoses.
Distinguish reducing from non-reducing sugars with examples, and explain why sucrose is non-reducing.
Describe the open-chain and cyclic structures of glucose and fructose, and the reactions that establish the structure of glucose.
Describe the structure of amino acids, the formation of the peptide bond, and the four levels of protein structure including denaturation.
Explain the action of enzymes and the elementary idea of hormones.
Classify vitamins as fat-soluble or water-soluble, and relate each to its function and deficiency disease.
Describe the structure of nucleic acids, the base pairing in DNA and the differences between DNA and RNA.

learn.title: Carbohydrates: definition, classification and reducing sugars

blocks.text: Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or polyhydroxy ketones, or compounds that give such units on hydrolysis. Their general formula is often written Cx(H2O)y, which is why the name means hydrate of carbon, although not every compound with that formula is a carbohydrate and not every carbohydrate fits it exactly. They are classified by the number of monosaccharide units they contain. Monosaccharides cannot be hydrolysed to simpler sugars and include glucose and fructose. Oligosaccharides contain two to ten units and include the disaccharides sucrose, lactose and maltose. Polysaccharides contain many units and include starch, cellulose and glycogen. Monosaccharides are further classified as aldoses if they contain an aldehyde group and ketoses if they contain a ketone group, and by the number of carbon atoms, so glucose is an aldohexose and fructose a ketohexose. Monosaccharides are also assigned D or L configuration by comparing the configuration at the penultimate (highest-numbered chiral) carbon with that of D-glyceraldehyde; most naturally occurring sugars, including D-glucose and D-fructose, belong to the D-series.

items.meaning: A sugar that cannot be hydrolysed into simpler sugars, for example glucose and fructose.
A sugar made of two monosaccharide units joined by a glycosidic bond, for example sucrose and maltose.
A large polymer of monosaccharide units, for example starch, cellulose and glycogen.
A monosaccharide containing an aldehyde group, such as glucose.
A monosaccharide containing a ketone group, such as fructose.
The oxygen linkage (glycosidic linkage) formed between the anomeric carbon of one sugar and a hydroxyl group of another; in a disaccharide it joins two monosaccharide units.

blocks.text: A reducing sugar is one that can reduce Tollens reagent or Fehling's solution, and the ability depends on whether the sugar has a free anomeric carbon that can open to the aldehyde or ketone form. Glucose, fructose, maltose and lactose are reducing sugars. Sucrose is not, because its glycosidic bond joins the anomeric carbon of glucose directly to the anomeric carbon of fructose, so neither ring can open and no aldehyde is available. On hydrolysis sucrose gives an equimolar mixture of glucose and fructose, which is called invert sugar because the originally dextrorotatory solution becomes laevorotatory as the fructose, which is strongly laevorotatory, is released. Mild oxidation of an aldose with bromine water confirms the aldehyde group, for example glucose gives gluconic acid: C6H12O6 + Br2 + H2O → C6H12O7 + 2HBr.

blocks.caption: Table: Important carbohydrates and their classification

items: Carbohydrates are the main source of energy for living organisms, and glucose is the fuel that cells oxidise directly.
Starch is the storage form of carbohydrate in plants and glycogen is the storage form in animals.
Cellulose is the structural material of plant cell walls and cannot be digested by humans, although it provides dietary fibre.
Ribose and deoxyribose are five-carbon sugars that form the backbone of nucleic acids.
Monosaccharides are sweet, soluble and crystalline, while polysaccharides are tasteless, insoluble and form colloidal dispersions.

learn.title: Glucose and fructose: structure and the reactions that establish it

blocks.text: Glucose has the molecular formula C6H12O6, and its open-chain structure is a straight chain of six carbon atoms carrying an aldehyde group at C1 and hydroxyl groups at C2 to C6. Each of the reactions used to establish this structure answers one question. Heating glucose with concentrated hydriodic acid reduces it to n-hexane, which shows that the six carbon atoms form an unbranched chain. Reaction with hydroxylamine gives an oxime and with hydrogen cyanide gives a cyanohydrin, which shows that a carbonyl group is present. Oxidation with bromine water gives gluconic acid, which shows that the carbonyl group is an aldehyde rather than a ketone. Reaction with acetic anhydride gives a penta-acetate, which shows that five hydroxyl groups are present. Oxidation with nitric acid gives saccharic acid, a dicarboxylic acid, which shows that the primary alcohol at C6 is at the other end of the chain from the aldehyde. Reaction with phenylhydrazine gives an osazone, which is used to identify the sugar.

The open-chain form is only a small part of the story, because glucose in solution exists mainly as a six-membered cyclic hemiacetal, formed when the hydroxyl group on C5 attacks the aldehyde carbon. The ring is drawn as a hexagon with oxygen in one corner, and the anomeric carbon, C1, carries a hydroxyl group that can point either down or up. The two arrangements are the alpha and beta anomers, and they interconvert through the open-chain form in solution, which is why a freshly dissolved pure anomer slowly changes its optical rotation until it reaches an equilibrium value; this is mutarotation. Fructose is a ketohexose with the same formula as glucose, and it also exists mainly in a cyclic form, but as a five-membered ring because it is the hydroxyl on C5 that attacks the ketone at C2.

items: Glucose with hydriodic acid gives n-hexane, proving an unbranched six-carbon chain.
Glucose with hydroxylamine gives glucose oxime, proving a carbonyl group.
Glucose with hydrogen cyanide gives a cyanohydrin, confirming the carbonyl group.
Glucose with bromine water gives gluconic acid, proving that the carbonyl group is an aldehyde.
Glucose with acetic anhydride gives glucose penta-acetate, proving five hydroxyl groups.
Glucose with nitric acid gives saccharic acid, proving a primary alcohol at the far end of the chain.
Glucose with phenylhydrazine gives glucosazone, a crystalline derivative used for identification.
Glucose reduces Tollens reagent and Fehling's solution, which is the basis of the test for a reducing sugar.
Bromine water oxidises glucose to gluconic acid but does not oxidise fructose, which distinguishes the two sugars.

items.text: How would you distinguish glucose from fructose using one chemical test?
items.note: Bromine water is decolourised by glucose, because it oxidises the aldehyde group to a carboxyl group and gives gluconic acid, while fructose, being a ketone, is not oxidised and does not decolourise the bromine water. Tollens reagent cannot be used because both sugars reduce it in alkaline solution.

items.text: Why does a freshly prepared solution of pure alpha-D-glucose gradually change its optical rotation?
items.note: The cyclic alpha form opens to the open-chain aldehyde and recloses to give a mixture of the alpha and beta anomers, which have different specific rotations. The rotation therefore drifts until the equilibrium mixture is reached, and this phenomenon is called mutarotation.

learn.title: Proteins: amino acids, peptide bonds and the four levels of structure

blocks.text: Proteins are polymers of alpha-amino acids, in which an amino group and a carboxyl group are attached to the same carbon, the alpha carbon, which also carries a hydrogen and a side chain. About twenty amino acids occur naturally, and they differ only in that side chain, which may be acidic, basic, polar or non-polar. Because each amino acid contains both an acidic and a basic group, it is amphoteric. In neutral aqueous solution it exists mainly as a zwitterion, with the carboxyl group deprotonated and the amino group protonated, so the molecule carries both a negative and a positive charge. The pH at which the number of positive and negative charges is equal is the isoelectric point, and at that pH the amino acid does not migrate in an electric field and is least soluble.

The carboxyl group of one amino acid reacts with the amino group of another, with the loss of water, to form an amide linkage called a peptide bond. Two amino acids joined this way give a dipeptide, three give a tripeptide, and a long chain gives a polypeptide. The chain has a free amino group at one end, the N-terminal end, and a free carboxyl group at the other, the C-terminal end, and the sequence of side chains along the chain is the primary structure of the protein. Secondary structure refers to the regular local folding of the chain into an alpha helix or a beta pleated sheet, held by hydrogen bonds between the carbonyl oxygen of one peptide bond and the N-H of another. Tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional shape produced by folding of the whole chain, held by interactions between side chains including disulphide bridges, hydrogen bonds, ionic attractions and hydrophobic effects. Quaternary structure describes the association of two or more polypeptide chains into a single functional protein, as in haemoglobin.

blocks.caption: Table: The four levels of protein structure
rows: the sequence of amino acids in the chain
local folding into alpha helices and beta pleated sheets
the overall three-dimensional shape of one chain
disulphide bonds, hydrogen bonds, ionic and hydrophobic interactions
the association of several chains into one protein

blocks.text: Denaturation is the loss of the secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure of a protein without breaking its peptide bonds. The primary structure remains intact, but the chain unfolds and the protein loses its biological activity. Denaturation is caused by heat, by extremes of pH, by alcohol, by heavy metal ions and by mechanical agitation, and it is usually irreversible. The classic example is the coagulation of egg white on boiling. Enzymes are proteins that act as biological catalysts, and their catalytic power depends on a specific region of the folded chain, the active site, which binds the substrate in a lock-and-key or induced-fit manner. Because the activity depends on the folded shape, denaturation destroys it. Hormones are chemical messengers secreted by endocrine glands, and the syllabus requires only an elementary idea: insulin is a protein hormone, while adrenaline and the sex hormones are not.

items: Amino acids are amphoteric because they contain both a basic amino group and an acidic carboxyl group.
The zwitterion carries -COO- and -NH3+ at the same time, so the molecule is electrically neutral overall.
The isoelectric point is the pH at which the amino acid has no net charge and does not move in an electric field.
Peptide bond formation is a condensation reaction that eliminates water between a carboxyl group and an amino group.
The N-terminal end of a polypeptide carries the free amino group and the C-terminal end carries the free carboxyl group.
Denaturation disrupts hydrogen bonds and disulphide bridges but leaves the peptide bonds intact, so the primary structure survives.
Enzymes are highly specific and are sensitive to temperature and pH because their activity depends on their folded shape.
Fibrous proteins such as keratin are long and insoluble and serve structural roles, while globular proteins such as haemoglobin are compact and soluble.

items.text: Why does a boiled egg never return to its raw state on cooling?
items.note: Heating denatures the egg-white proteins, disrupting the hydrogen bonds and other interactions that hold the chain in its folded shape. The unfolded chains aggregate and coagulate, and because the new arrangement is stabilised by many interactions between chains, cooling cannot restore the original folded structure, so the change is irreversible.

items.text: Why does an enzyme lose its activity when the pH is changed far from its optimum?
items.note: The side chains of the amino acids at the active site must be in specific ionisation states to bind the substrate and to catalyse the reaction. Changing the pH alters which groups are protonated, so the active site changes shape and the substrate no longer binds, which is a form of denaturation.

learn.title: Vitamins: classification, functions and deficiency diseases

blocks.text: Vitamins are organic compounds required in small amounts for normal growth and metabolism, which the body cannot synthesise in sufficient quantity and must therefore obtain from the diet. They are classified by solubility, which also predicts how they are absorbed and stored. The fat-soluble vitamins are A, D, E and K; they are absorbed with dietary fats, stored in the liver and in fatty tissue, and an excess can accumulate to toxic levels. The water-soluble vitamins are the B group and vitamin C; they are absorbed with water, any excess is excreted in the urine, and they must therefore be supplied regularly because they cannot be stored in large amounts.

cheilosis and inflammation of the tongue

antioxidant and cofactor in the synthesis of collagen

required for the synthesis of clotting factors

items: Fat-soluble vitamins are A, D, E and K, and they are stored in the liver and fatty tissue.
Water-soluble vitamins are the B group and C, and excess is excreted in urine, so regular intake is needed.
Vitamin A is derived from beta-carotene and is essential for vision in dim light.
Vitamin D is made in the skin on exposure to sunlight, so deficiency is common where exposure is limited.
Vitamin C is required for the hydroxylation of proline in collagen, which is why deficiency causes bleeding gums and poor wound healing.
Vitamin K is needed for the gamma-carboxylation of glutamate residues in clotting factors.

items.text: Why does a diet lacking fresh fruit and vegetables cause scurvy but not night blindness?
items.note: Fresh fruit and vegetables are the main dietary source of vitamin C, which is water-soluble and cannot be stored, so a deficiency develops within weeks and gives scurvy. Night blindness results from a lack of vitamin A, which is obtained mainly from dairy products, liver and beta-carotene-rich vegetables, so the two deficiencies have different dietary causes.

items.text: Why can an overdose of vitamin A be harmful while an excess of vitamin C is usually not?
items.note: Vitamin A is fat-soluble and is stored in the liver, so repeated large doses accumulate and can cause toxicity. Vitamin C is water-soluble, so any excess beyond the body needs is excreted in the urine and does not accumulate.

learn.title: Nucleic acids: nucleotides, the DNA double helix and the difference from RNA

blocks.text: Nucleic acids are polymers of nucleotides, and each nucleotide is made of three parts: a pentose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base. The bases are of two kinds. The purines, adenine and guanine, have a fused two-ring structure, while the pyrimidines, cytosine, thymine and uracil, have a single ring. The sugar in DNA is deoxyribose and the sugar in RNA is ribose, and the difference between them is a single oxygen, since ribose has a hydroxyl group at the 2' position that deoxyribose lacks. Nucleotides are joined into a chain by phosphodiester bonds between the phosphate of one nucleotide and the sugar of the next, so the backbone of the polymer is a sugar-phosphate chain with the bases projecting from it.

The structure of DNA is a double helix of two antiparallel chains wound around a common axis. The bases of one chain point inwards and pair with the bases of the other through hydrogen bonds, and the pairing is specific: adenine pairs with thymine by two hydrogen bonds, and guanine pairs with cytosine by three. This specificity means that the sequence of one chain determines the sequence of the other, which is how DNA replicates and how genetic information is preserved. RNA is usually single-stranded, contains ribose in place of deoxyribose, and contains uracil in place of thymine. There are three main kinds of RNA: messenger RNA carries the genetic message from DNA to the ribosome, transfer RNA brings amino acids to the ribosome, and ribosomal RNA forms part of the ribosome itself.

blocks.caption: Table: Differences between DNA and RNA
rows: A with T, G with C
mainly in the cytoplasm and at the ribosome
storage and transmission of genetic information

items: A nucleotide consists of a pentose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base.
The purines are adenine and guanine, and the pyrimidines are cytosine, thymine and uracil.
Nucleotides are linked by phosphodiester bonds, giving a sugar-phosphate backbone.
In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine and guanine with cytosine, so the two chains are complementary.
The two strands of the DNA double helix run in opposite directions, which is described as antiparallel.
RNA contains uracil instead of thymine and ribose instead of deoxyribose, and it is usually single-stranded.
Messenger RNA carries the code, transfer RNA delivers amino acids, and ribosomal RNA forms part of the ribosome.
The sequence of bases in DNA determines the sequence of amino acids in a protein through the genetic code.

items.text: If one strand of a DNA double helix has the sequence A-T-G-C-C-A, what is the sequence of the complementary strand?
items.note: A pairs with T, T with A, G with C, C with G, C with G and A with T, so the complementary sequence is T-A-C-G-G-T. The two strands are antiparallel, so the complementary strand is read in the opposite direction.

items.text: Why is DNA a better molecule than RNA for storing genetic information?
items.note: DNA is double-stranded, so each strand can serve as a template for repairing the other, and the absence of the 2' hydroxyl group in deoxyribose makes DNA chemically more stable than RNA, whose hydroxyl group makes it prone to hydrolysis. RNA is therefore used as a short-lived working copy rather than as the permanent store.

keyPoints: Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes and ketones, classified as monosaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides, and as aldoses and ketoses.
Reducing sugars have a free anomeric carbon; sucrose is non-reducing because both anomeric carbons are involved in the glycosidic bond.
Glucose is an aldohexose with an unbranched six-carbon chain, one aldehyde group and five hydroxyl groups.
The reactions of glucose with hydriodic acid, bromine water, acetic anhydride, nitric acid and phenylhydrazine each establish one feature of its structure.
Glucose exists mainly as a cyclic hemiacetal, and the interconversion of its alpha and beta anomers causes mutarotation.
Amino acids are amphoteric and exist as zwitterions, with an isoelectric point at which they carry no net charge.
Proteins have four levels of structure, and denaturation destroys the higher levels without breaking peptide bonds.
Fat-soluble vitamins are A, D, E and K, and water-soluble vitamins are the B group and C, each with a characteristic deficiency disease.
A nucleotide consists of a pentose sugar, a phosphate and a nitrogenous base, joined into chains by phosphodiester bonds.
DNA is a double helix with deoxyribose and thymine, pairing A with T and G with C, while RNA is single-stranded with ribose and uracil.

The linkage between the anomeric carbon of one sugar and a hydroxyl group of another, formed with loss of water.
The gradual change in optical rotation of a sugar solution as the alpha and beta anomers equilibrate through the open-chain form.
The crystalline derivative formed when a reducing sugar reacts with phenylhydrazine, used to identify the sugar.
A compound containing both an amino group and a carboxyl group on the same carbon, the monomer of proteins.
A species carrying both a positive and a negative charge at the same time, as an amino acid does in neutral solution.

questions.prompt: Glucose is best described as:
options: an aldohexose
a ketohexose
an aldopentose
a disaccharide
questions.answer: an aldohexose
questions.explanation: Glucose has six carbon atoms and contains an aldehyde group at C1, so it is an aldohexose. Fructose, with the same formula but a ketone group at C2, is the corresponding ketohexose.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing glucose with fructose, which is the ketohexose.

questions.prompt: Sucrose is a non-reducing sugar because:
options: it does not dissolve in water
its glycosidic bond involves the anomeric carbons of both monosaccharides, so neither ring can open
it contains no hydroxyl groups
it is a polysaccharide rather than a disaccharide
questions.answer: its glycosidic bond involves the anomeric carbons of both monosaccharides, so neither ring can open
questions.explanation: Reducing power requires a free anomeric carbon that can open to the aldehyde form. In sucrose the anomeric carbon of glucose and that of fructose are both used in the glycosidic bond, so no such carbon is available and the sugar cannot reduce Tollens or Fehling's reagent.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming that all disaccharides are reducing, when maltose and lactose are but sucrose is not.

questions.prompt: Which sugar reduces Tollens reagent but does not decolourise bromine water?
options: Maltose
Lactose
Fructose
Glucose
questions.answer: Fructose
questions.explanation: Fructose is a ketose, so bromine water, which is a mild oxidant, cannot oxidise it and its colour remains. In the alkaline conditions of Tollens reagent, however, fructose tautomerises through an enediol into glucose and mannose, which are aldoses, and these reduce the silver ion, so a positive test is observed.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming that a ketose cannot reduce Tollens reagent at all.

questions.prompt: The peptide bond in a protein is formed between:
options: the amino groups of two amino acids
the carboxyl groups of two amino acids
the side chains of two amino acids
the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of another
questions.answer: the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of another
questions.explanation: The carboxyl group of one amino acid loses a hydroxyl group and the amino group of the next loses a hydrogen, and the two combine with elimination of water to give the amide linkage -CO-NH-, which is the peptide bond.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing the peptide bond with a hydrogen bond between side chains, which helps hold the folded structure but does not join the monomers.

questions.prompt: Deficiency of vitamin C causes:
options: scurvy
rickets
beri-beri
night blindness
questions.answer: scurvy
questions.explanation: Vitamin C is needed for the hydroxylation of proline in the synthesis of collagen, so its deficiency weakens connective tissue and causes scurvy, with bleeding gums and poor wound healing. Rickets is caused by a deficiency of vitamin D, beri-beri by thiamine, and night blindness by vitamin A.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing the deficiency diseases of the fat-soluble and water-soluble vitamins.

questions.prompt: Which statement about DNA is correct?
options: It contains ribose and thymine and is double-stranded
It contains deoxyribose and thymine and is double-stranded
It contains ribose and uracil and is single-stranded
It contains deoxyribose and uracil and is single-stranded
questions.answer: It contains deoxyribose and thymine and is double-stranded
questions.explanation: DNA has deoxyribose as its sugar, uses thymine as one of its pyrimidines and exists as a double helix. RNA has ribose, uses uracil instead of thymine and is usually single-stranded.
questions.commonMistake: Mixing the sugar and the base, for example giving DNA ribose or uracil.

questions.prompt: Bromine water distinguishes glucose from fructose because:
options: neither reacts, but glucose dissolves the bromine
fructose decolourises bromine water by oxidation to gluconic acid, while glucose does not
glucose decolourises bromine water by oxidation to gluconic acid, while fructose does not
both decolourise it, but at different rates
questions.answer: glucose decolourises bromine water by oxidation to gluconic acid, while fructose does not
questions.explanation: Bromine water is a mild oxidant that oxidises the aldehyde group of glucose to a carboxyl group, giving gluconic acid and decolourising the solution. Fructose is a ketone and is not oxidised under these mild conditions, so the colour persists.
questions.commonMistake: Using Tollens reagent for this distinction, which both sugars reduce.

questions.prompt: Denaturation of a protein involves:
options: formation of new peptide bonds between chains
conversion of the amino acids into fatty acids
hydrolysis of the peptide bonds into amino acids
loss of secondary and tertiary structure without breaking peptide bonds
questions.answer: loss of secondary and tertiary structure without breaking peptide bonds
questions.explanation: Denaturation disrupts the hydrogen bonds, disulphide bridges and other interactions that maintain the folded shape, so the chain unfolds and the protein loses its activity, but the peptide bonds along the chain remain intact. Hydrolysis of peptide bonds would break the protein into amino acids, which is a different process.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking that denaturation breaks the primary structure.

questions.prompt: The linkage joining two amino acids in a protein is called a ______ bond.
questions.answer: peptide
questions.explanation: The amide linkage formed by condensation between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next is the peptide bond, and a chain of many such bonds gives a polypeptide.
questions.commonMistake: Writing glycosidic, which joins sugars rather than amino acids.

questions.prompt: Glucose heated with concentrated hydriodic acid is reduced to ______, which shows that its six carbon atoms form an unbranched chain.
questions.answer: n-hexane
questions.explanation: Hydriodic acid reduces glucose completely, replacing all the oxygen functions by hydrogen, and the product is n-hexane. Because the product is an unbranched six-carbon alkane, the carbon skeleton of glucose must be a straight chain.
questions.commonMistake: Writing hexanoic acid, which would retain a carboxyl group that hydriodic acid removes.

questions.prompt: Deficiency of vitamin D in children causes ______.
questions.answer: rickets
questions.explanation: Vitamin D promotes the absorption of calcium and phosphate, so its deficiency leads to poor mineralisation of bone. In children this produces rickets, with soft and deformed bones, and in adults it produces osteomalacia.
questions.commonMistake: Writing scurvy, which is the vitamin C deficiency disease.

questions.prompt: Define the isoelectric point of an amino acid and state its significance.
questions.answer: The isoelectric point is the pH at which an amino acid carries equal numbers of positive and negative charges, so that the molecule has no net charge and exists mainly as its zwitterion. At this pH the amino acid does not migrate towards either electrode in an electric field, and it is at its minimum solubility, which is why the isoelectric point is used in electrophoresis and in the precipitation of proteins.
questions.explanation: The definition combines the charge balance with its two practical consequences, no migration in an electric field and minimum solubility.
questions.commonMistake: Describing the isoelectric point as the pH at which the amino acid carries no charge at all, when it carries equal and opposite charges.

questions.prompt: Explain why sucrose is non-reducing while maltose is reducing.
questions.answer: A sugar is reducing only if it has a free anomeric carbon that can open to give an aldehyde group. In sucrose the glycosidic bond joins the anomeric carbon of glucose to the anomeric carbon of fructose, so both anomeric centres are locked in the linkage and neither ring can open. In maltose the glycosidic bond joins the anomeric carbon of one glucose unit to an ordinary hydroxyl group of the other, so the second unit still has a free anomeric carbon and can reduce Tollens and Fehling's reagents.
questions.explanation: The difference is entirely about whether both anomeric carbons are used in the glycosidic bond or only one, which decides whether a reducing group remains available.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming that all disaccharides behave alike, when sucrose is the exception.

questions.prompt: Give two differences between DNA and RNA.
questions.answer: First, DNA contains the sugar deoxyribose and the pyrimidine thymine, whereas RNA contains ribose and uracil in place of thymine. Second, DNA is double-stranded and forms a double helix, while RNA is usually single-stranded. DNA stores and transmits genetic information, whereas RNA carries out protein synthesis.
questions.explanation: The sugar and the base are the two structural differences that are always asked, and the strandedness and function follow from them.
questions.commonMistake: Giving two differences that both concern the bases, when the sugar difference should be included.

questions.prompt: What is denaturation of a protein, and why is it usually irreversible?
questions.answer: Denaturation is the loss of the secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure of a protein without breaking its peptide bonds, so the chain unfolds and the protein loses its biological activity. It is usually irreversible because the unfolded chains aggregate with one another through many new interactions, forming a stable coagulated mass that cannot refold into the original precise three-dimensional structure. The primary structure is unchanged, but the information needed to specify the fold is not enough to restore it once aggregation has occurred.
questions.explanation: The irreversibility comes from aggregation between unfolded chains, not from any change in the peptide sequence.
questions.commonMistake: Saying that denaturation breaks the protein into amino acids, which would be hydrolysis.

questions.prompt: Describe the reactions used to establish the open-chain structure of glucose, stating what each reaction proves.
questions.answer: Heating glucose with concentrated hydriodic acid gives n-hexane, which proves that the six carbon atoms form an unbranched chain. Reaction with hydroxylamine gives an oxime and with hydrogen cyanide gives a cyanohydrin, both of which prove the presence of a carbonyl group. Oxidation with bromine water gives gluconic acid, which proves that the carbonyl group is an aldehyde rather than a ketone. Reaction with acetic anhydride gives glucose penta-acetate, which proves the presence of five hydroxyl groups. Oxidation with nitric acid gives saccharic acid, a dicarboxylic acid, which proves that a primary alcohol group lies at the opposite end of the chain from the aldehyde. Reaction with phenylhydrazine gives glucosazone, a crystalline derivative used to identify the sugar.
questions.explanation: Each reaction answers a specific structural question, so the complete structure is built up by combining the conclusions rather than by any single experiment.
questions.commonMistake: Listing the reactions without stating what each one proves, which is what the question actually asks.

questions.prompt: Describe the four levels of protein structure and explain what happens to each of them during denaturation.
questions.answer: The primary structure is the sequence of amino acids along the chain, held together by peptide bonds. The secondary structure is the regular local folding of the chain into alpha helices and beta pleated sheets, held by hydrogen bonds between the carbonyl oxygen of one peptide group and the N-H of another. The tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional shape of the folded chain, held by disulphide bridges, hydrogen bonds, ionic attractions and hydrophobic interactions between side chains. The quaternary structure is the association of two or more polypeptide chains into one functional protein, as in haemoglobin. During denaturation the hydrogen bonds and other interactions holding the secondary, tertiary and quaternary structures are disrupted, so the chain unfolds and the protein loses its activity, but the peptide bonds remain intact and the primary structure is unchanged.
questions.explanation: Denaturation is defined by exactly this pattern, the loss of the higher levels of structure while the primary sequence survives.
questions.commonMistake: Including the primary structure among the levels destroyed by denaturation.

questions.prompt: Classify vitamins by solubility and give the function and deficiency disease of one vitamin from each class.
questions.answer: Vitamins are classified as fat-soluble and water-soluble. The fat-soluble vitamins are A, D, E and K; they are absorbed with dietary fats and stored in the liver and fatty tissue. Vitamin A is needed for the formation of rhodopsin and for healthy epithelium, and its deficiency causes night blindness and xerophthalmia. The water-soluble vitamins are the B group and vitamin C; they are absorbed with water and any excess is excreted, so they must be supplied regularly. Vitamin C is required for the synthesis of collagen and acts as an antioxidant, and its deficiency causes scurvy, with bleeding gums and poor wound healing. Other examples are vitamin D, whose deficiency causes rickets, and thiamine, whose deficiency causes beri-beri.
questions.explanation: Solubility determines absorption and storage, which in turn determines whether a deficiency develops quickly or slowly and whether an excess can be toxic.
questions.commonMistake: Giving the deficiency disease without the function, when the question asks for both.

questions.prompt: Glucose is treated separately with bromine water, nitric acid, acetic anhydride and phenylhydrazine. State the product in each case and what the reaction establishes about the structure of glucose.
questions.answer: With bromine water glucose gives gluconic acid, which establishes that the carbonyl group is an aldehyde, since a mild oxidant converts it to a carboxyl group. With nitric acid glucose gives saccharic acid, a dicarboxylic acid, which establishes that the primary alcohol group at C6 lies at the opposite end of the chain from the aldehyde. With acetic anhydride glucose gives glucose penta-acetate, which establishes that five hydroxyl groups are present. With phenylhydrazine glucose gives glucosazone, a crystalline derivative used to identify the sugar and to show that the carbonyl group is adjacent to a carbon bearing a hydroxyl group.
questions.explanation: The four reagents probe different features, the aldehyde end, the other end, the hydroxyl count and the carbonyl environment, so together they pin down the open-chain structure.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing gluconic acid, from mild oxidation, with saccharic acid, from oxidation of both ends.

questions.prompt: Fructose is a ketose, yet it reduces Tollens and Fehling's reagents. Explain this apparent contradiction.
questions.answer: In the alkaline medium of Tollens and Fehling's reagents, fructose undergoes tautomerisation through an enediol intermediate into glucose and mannose, both of which are aldoses. The aldehyde groups of these aldoses are then available to reduce the silver ion or the copper(II) complex, so a positive test is observed even though fructose itself has no aldehyde group. The reduction is therefore caused by the isomerisation products rather than by fructose as such, which is why fructose reduces these reagents but does not decolourise bromine water, since bromine water is used under conditions too mild to bring about the isomerisation.
questions.explanation: The contradiction is resolved by the difference between the alkaline oxidising reagents and the mildly acidic bromine water, which selects which reaction pathway is available.
questions.commonMistake: Stating that fructose contains an aldehyde group, which it does not.

questions.prompt: A carbohydrate of molecular formula C6H12O6 reduces Tollens reagent but does not decolourise bromine water, and it gives the same osazone as glucose. Identify it and explain each observation.
questions.answer: The compound is fructose. The molecular formula corresponds to a hexose, and it reduces Tollens reagent, which is consistent with a reducing sugar. It does not decolourise bromine water, which shows that it is a ketose rather than an aldose, since bromine water oxidises only the aldehyde group. It gives the same osazone as glucose because the reaction with phenylhydrazine involves the carbon atoms C1 and C2 and destroys the difference between an aldose and a ketose at those positions, so glucose and fructose give the same osazone.
questions.explanation: The three observations together fix fructose: the formula limits it to a hexose, the bromine water result identifies the ketone, and the osazone confirms the relationship with glucose.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing glucose, which would decolourise bromine water.

questions.prompt: Starch and cellulose are both polymers of glucose, yet humans can digest starch but not cellulose. Explain the structural reason.
questions.answer: Starch is a polymer of alpha-glucose joined by alpha-1,4 glycosidic bonds, with branches through alpha-1,6 bonds, and the alpha linkage gives a coiled chain that the enzyme amylase can hydrolyse. Cellulose is a polymer of beta-glucose joined by beta-1,4 glycosidic bonds, and the beta linkage makes the chain straight and allows it to pack into strong fibres held by hydrogen bonds. Human digestive enzymes are specific for the alpha linkage and cannot hydrolyse the beta linkage, so cellulose passes through the digestive tract unchanged as dietary fibre, while starch is broken down into glucose.
questions.explanation: The difference is not in the monomer, which is glucose in both cases, but in the configuration of the glycosidic bond, which the enzymes recognise.
questions.commonMistake: Saying that cellulose is not a carbohydrate or that it contains a different sugar, when the monomer is glucose in both polymers.
